I’ve been reflecting lately on the ways in which technology and creativity intersect, particularly as they relate to artificial intelligence. It’s fascinating to think that just a decade or two ago, the idea of a computer spontaneously generating music, painting, or writing was little more than a curiosity—or a science fiction trope. Yet here we are, in an era where AI can analyze patterns and produce surprisingly compelling art, music, and text.

One of the most exciting things about AI is its ability to free up creative energy. Picture a filmmaker who can quickly use AI-based tools to do initial scene concepts or rough storyboarding, then focus more on refining the narrative, dialogue, and emotional nuances that only a human can perfect. Or imagine a composer who has the support of an AI engine that suggests chord progressions matching a particular mood, leaving the composer more mental bandwidth to innovate with melody and thematic development. 

These glimpses of AI-assisted creativity invite us to consider how we define originality. After all, an AI is “inspired” by the data it was trained on—whether that’s a million images on the internet or a massive library of classical music. There’s an ongoing debate about whether that constitutes genuine creativity or merely rearrangement. Regardless of one’s stance, I think it underscores an essential truth: creativity doesn’t happen in a vacuum. Even when humans come up with brilliant ideas, we build on everything we’ve seen, heard, or experienced. We stand on the shoulders of cultural giants—just as AI stands on the shoulders of countless inputs fed into its models.

Of course, there are ethical considerations. Automation can reduce tedious tasks, but it can also disrupt entire industries. People whose livelihoods depend on certain forms of repetitive or formulaic creation might find themselves in the unenviable position of competing with AI tools that can churn out content in seconds. And then there are questions of intellectual property: if you train an AI on existing artwork or text, to what extent does that training material belong to the AI’s owner versus the original creator?

At the same time, it’s exhilarating to see the doors that AI opens in science, accessibility, and social impact. We’re seeing medical breakthroughs where AI assists in diagnosing diseases far earlier than human eyes can detect. We’re seeing language translation tools that allow for near-instant communication across vast linguistic divides. And while early attempts at text-to-speech or speech-to-text were once comically inaccurate, modern systems let individuals with disabilities communicate more effectively and navigate the world in ways previously unthinkable.

Even in the realm of entertainment and leisure, AI is steadily reshaping how we spend our free time—automating the compositional aspects of video games, generating virtual characters on the fly, creating entire environments that adapt to the player’s actions. This capacity for adaptation is, in my view, one of AI’s most appealing aspects. What might our digital experiences look like when each user can experience a tailor-made environment that reacts to their preferences and needs?

From these perspectives, AI clearly offers us the opportunity to enhance our humanity if we are careful and conscientious in how we use it. The real challenge is ensuring that the technology remains at our service, rather than allowing ourselves to become servants to it. Striking this balance—between harnessing AI’s power for creative, scientific, and economic benefits, and maintaining our autonomy and ethics—will be an ongoing conversation for years to come.

In the end, I think the most powerful statement we can make about AI is that it’s less about machine-versus-human and more about synergy. We often frame it as a competition or a futuristic robot takeover scenario, but in reality, AI tools in human hands enable us to tackle challenges with greater nuance, insight, and speed. And that is something profoundly hopeful. After all, every new technology in history has carried with it a wave of changes and concerns—yet we also gain immense benefits. If we navigate carefully and thoughtfully, I believe AI will be a driving force for positive transformation, creativity, and progress in the decades ahead.
